w3_open: People think a chair moving on its own would be... funny. [exhales] It was the most frightening thing I have ever seen.
w3_s1: It came over the radio as a domestic disturbance. It was nothing of the sort. The mother met us at the door — I remember her hands. She couldn't keep them still. And the children were sat on the stairs, in a row. Silent. [pause] Children that frightened don't cry. They go quiet.
w3_s2: We stood in the front room, and we waited. I felt a bit of a fool, honestly. Stood in someone's front room, waiting for furniture. [exhales] And then the chair went. It wobbled — side to side — and then it slid. Across the floor, towards the kitchen wall. Three feet, maybe four. And then it stopped. ... Like it had done what it came to do. Nobody was anywhere near it.
w3_s3: I went over that chair like it was evidence. Underneath. The carpet. Looking for wires, thread... anything. There was nothing. And I remember kneeling there, thinking — I'm going to have to put this in a statement. And nobody is ever going to believe me.
w3_s4: You can't arrest a chair. [soft laugh] We told her it wasn't a police matter. Which is what you say, when you have nothing else to say. And we left them there. Four children, on the stairs. ... That's the part I think about.
w3_s5: I signed my statement because it was true. People have laughed at it for fifty years. [sighs] The air in that room went... wrong. I've never been able to describe it better than that. The chair moved. Nothing touched it. And I was sober, on duty, in uniform. ... Make of it what you like.
